title: Paramananda Puri
html:
A Brahmana of Trihut

Sri Paramananda Puri was a sannyasi, a disciple of Sri Madhavendra Puri, and one of Mahaprabhu’s closest companions in Nilachala. Vrindavana Dasa Thakura, listing those who came into the world before the Lord, says of him:

“Sri Paramananda Puri, the intimate companion of Sri Chaitanya in Nilachala, was born in Trihut.” (CB, Adi 2.43)

Trihut, or Tirhut, is the northern part of present-day Bihar — the districts of Muzaffarpur, Darbhanga, Sitamarhi, Champaran and Chhapra; in ancient times it was a kingdom of its own. Another disciple of Madhavendra, the scholar Raghupati Upadhyaya, also came from Tirhut. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati speaks of Paramananda Puri first of all as “a brahmana born in Trihut,” and in his “Anubhashya” on the “Charitamrita” writes of him: “a brahmana from Trihut, a disciple of Sri Madhavendra Puri and very dear to Mahaprabhu.”

Nothing more is known of his worldly life. The sources name neither his parents nor the year and day of his appearance, nor when and where he left this world; nor are the days of his appearance and disappearance found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. We know only that he outlived Mahaprabhu: after the Lord’s disappearance Srinivasa Acharya still found him in Puri.

The “Charitamrita” calls him Paramananda Puri and Puri Gosani, and sometimes simply “Puri”; Vrindavana Dasa calls him Puri Gosani and Puri Gosvami; Kavi Karnapura, in the drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” calls him Paramananda Puri-ishvara and Puri-ishvara, “the lord of the Puris”; the biographies add the honorifics “Puripada” and “Sri Paramananda Puripada.”

Uddhava

Who he is in the eternal pastimes of Krishna, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“Sri Paramananda Puri was formerly Uddhava.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 118)

The Uddhava of Krishna’s pastimes descended into Gaura’s pastimes as Paramananda Puri, to enrich them with his service. This is no rebirth: an eternal associate of the Lord descends into the world together with Him and by His will. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, too, calls him Uddhava, and so do the Vaishnava vandanas: the “Vaishnava-vandana” ascribed to Jiva Gosvami praises “Sri Puri Paramananda, called Uddhava, dear to Hari” (1.58), Devakinandana praises him “who is Uddhava by nature” (2.46), and the vandana ascribed to the “second” Vrindavana Dasa, “him whom they call Thakura Uddhava.” The same Sanskrit vandana speaks of the sannyasi companions of the Lord “headed by Sri Paramananda Puri” (1.141).1

A Disciple of Madhavendra Puri

Paramananda Puri received initiation from Sri Madhavendra Puri. Vrindavana Dasa says of him:

“Sri Paramananda Puri was a dear disciple of Sri Madhavendra Puri, and he was brimming with the sweetness of divine love.” (CB, Antya 3.178)

So too do Murari Gupta — “a disciple of Sri Madhava Puri named Paramananda” (3.15.19), Lochana Dasa (CM, Shesha-khanda, pt. 2, v. 136) and Karnapura — “a disciple of the lord of sages, Madhavendra Puri” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” act 8). Among Madhavendra’s other disciples are named Ishvara Puri, the guru of Mahaprabhu, Advaita Acharya, Brahmananda Puri, Sri Ranga Puri, Pundarika Vidyanidhi, Raghupati Upadhyaya and others.

The title “Puri” is the name of one of the ten orders of sannyasis, but Paramananda Puri was no Mayavadi renunciate seeking to merge into the impersonal Brahman. He was a Vaishnava sannyasi in the line of Madhavendra, and his whole wealth was prema, love for Krishna: Vrindavana Dasa calls him “the abode of pure love for Sri Chaitanya” (CB, Antya 3.175).

As a disciple of Madhavendra he was a godbrother of Ishvara Puri, the Lord’s guru. Therefore Mahaprabhu showed him the highest respect: He regarded him as a most beloved elder and honoured him as His own guru. It was his connection with Madhavendra Puri, the biographies say, that made him an object of such reverence for the Lord. The Lord Himself, the Master of all, is above every guru; but, setting an example for the world, He honoured the guru-varga — the circle of His elders — and taught others by doing so.

The Central Root of the Tree

Describing the tree of bhakti grown by Sri Chaitanya, Krishnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami says:

“Glory to Sri Madhava Puri, brimming with love for Krishna! He is the first sprout of the wish-fulfilling tree of bhakti. In the form of Sri Ishvara Puri the sprout grew strong, and then the gardener, Sri Chaitanya Himself, became the trunk of the tree. By His own inconceivable power the gardener became the trunk, the original support of all the branches.” (CC, Adi 9.10–12)2

Herein lies the supreme secret of the tree: the Lord is both its gardener and its trunk, and all this by the power of His inconceivable energy. And at the base of the tree nine roots sprang up — nine sannyasis:

“At the base of the tree nine roots sprang up: Paramananda Puri and Keshava Bharati, Brahmananda Puri and Brahmananda Bharati, Vishnu Puri, Keshava Puri, Krishnananda Puri, Sri Nrisimha Tirtha and Sukhananda Puri. On them the tree stood immovable. The central root is Paramananda Puri, a man of great steadfastness, and on these nine roots the tree stood secure.” (CC, Adi 9.13–16)3

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in his “Anubhashya” makes this a subheading: “Paramananda Puri, the middle root.”

The Meeting on Rishabha Hill

Mahaprabhu first met Paramananda Puri on His pilgrimage to the South. Leaving Purushottama, the Lord passed through Kurmasthana, Jiyada-Nrisimha, Vidyanagara, where He conversed with Ramananda Raya, the Gautami-Ganga, Mallikarjuna, Ahobala, Siddhavata, Skanda-kshetra, Trimatha, Vriddha-Kashi, Bauddhasthana, Tirupati, Trimalla, Pana-Nrisimha, Shiva-Kanchi and Vishnu-Kanchi, Trikalahasti, Vriddhakola, Shiyali-Bhairavi, the banks of the Kaveri, Kumbhakarna-kapala and Srirangam, where He spent the four months of the rains with Venkata Bhatta and blessed his whole family. After the chaturmasya He went on further south — and came to Rishabha hill.

Rishabha hill lies in the South of India, near Madurai. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, as the biographies report, describes the place thus: twelve miles north of Madurai are the Anagadamalai hills, in the forests around Kutakachala, where, according to tradition, Rishabhadeva perished in a forest fire; today it is known as Palni Hill, and the local people call it Varaha-parvata.4

The “Charitamrita” relates:

“Gaurahari went on and came to Rishabha hill. There He saw Narayana and offered obeisances and prayers. Paramananda Puri was staying there for the four months. Hearing this, Mahaprabhu went to Puri Gosani. The Lord bowed at the feet of Puri Gosani, and Puri Gosani lovingly embraced Him.” (CC, Madhya 9.167–169)

Paramananda Puri was keeping his chaturmasya vow there, living in the house of a brahmana. The Lord too stayed in that same house, and for three days they spoke of Krishna, filled with the bliss of prema (Madhya 9.170). Krishnadasa Kaviraja mentions this meeting in his summary of the pastimes as well: “Travelling through South India, He met Paramananda Puri” (Madhya 1.111).

On parting, Puri said that he was going to Purushottama to see Jagannatha, and from there on to Gauda for a bath in the Ganga. Then the Lord asked him:

“‘Please come back to Nilachala. I shall return from Setubandha before long. I wish to stay in your company, so be kind to Me and come to Nilachala.’ Having said this and taken his leave, the Lord went on to the south in great joy. Paramananda Puri then set out for Nilachala, and Mahaprabhu went on and came to Sri Shaila.” (CC, Madhya 9.172–175)

The Lord wished Puri to come to Nilachala and stay there with Him for good.

Other original sources tell of this meeting differently and with new details.5 According to Murari Gupta, the Lord met Paramananda Puri on the road from Ranga-kshetra:

“Seeing the form of Gauranga, Sri Paramananda Puri remembered his guru’s words, and was adorned with tears of love and thrilling hair. And the Lord too, the guardian of dharma, in supreme delight fell down like a stick, His head to the ground, before Puripada and his servant. In alarm Puri said, ‘You should not do so! You alone are the Lord of the worlds, the One who awakens consciousness in the world. I know who You are: You are Bhagavan Himself, who has taken the form of a devotee of Sri Krishna; You have assumed the mood of Sri Radha and thirst for the rasa of sweetness.’ Hearing his words, Krishna laughed and replied respectfully, ‘Know that My heart is bound by your love — of this there is no doubt. Go to the most delightful Kshetra and stay there until I return.’” (Murari Gupta, 3.15.20–25)

Lochana Dasa says that, looking at the Lord, Paramananda Puri remembered his guru’s prophecy. Madhavendra had once told him: in the first twilight of Kali the Lord of Lakshmi will appear — a golden-bodied sannyasi dwelling near the Daru-brahma; “I have not the good fortune to see Him with my own eyes; when you see Him, remember me.” And Puri understood firmly: this is Bhagavan Himself. In tears he kept repeating “Madhavendra!” — and the Lord, hearing the name of Madhavendra, danced and wept in bliss:

“‘Today My sannyasa has borne fruit: the name of Madhavendra has entered My ears.’” (CM, Shesha-khanda, pt. 2, v. 142+4)6

Puri bowed to Him, and the Lord, saying “What are you doing?”, lifted him up and embraced him tightly (vv. 134–144). Lochana Dasa places the meeting after the chaturmasya, on the road from Trimalla; so too does a biography that retells his poem: the Lord spent four months in Srirangam, then met Paramananda Puri, who offered prayers to Gaura.

Kavi Karnapura in his mahakavya makes a riddle of his name: the Lord met the best of ascetics, at the beginning of whose name was “Parama,” in the middle “ananda,” and at the end “Puri”; then Paramananda went to Puri, and the Lord to the Setu (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 13.14–16). Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” writes that on Rishabha hill, near Narayana, “the ascetic Paramananda” spent the four months of the rains, and that the Lord met and honoured him (10.12–13); the “Karcha” of Govinda Dasa likewise says, “On Rishabha hill lives Paramananda Puri,” and the Lord hastened to see him (6.1100–1102).

Through Gauda to Nilachala

After a few more days on Rishabha hill, Paramananda Puri went, as he had intended, to the Ganga, and, walking along its bank, came to Navadvipa:

“At that time Paramananda Puri, coming from the south along the bank of the Ganga, arrived in the town of Nadiya. He stayed happily in mother Shachi's house, and she respectfully gave him his meal.” (CC, Madhya 10.91–92)

He lived in Mayapur, in the house of Shachimata, and took his meals from her hands, and she looked after him with great love.

Meanwhile Mahaprabhu had returned from the South to Puri. Nityananda, Jagadananda, Mukunda and Damodara resolved to inform Shachimata and the Bengali devotees of His return, and, with the Lord’s permission, sent to Gauda Kala Krishnadasa, the Lord’s companion on His southern journey (CC, Madhya 10.67–72).7 The news spread through Gauda, and Advaita Acharya and the other devotees, taking leave of Shachi, began to prepare for the journey to Nilachala (10.88).

Paramananda Puri too heard the news. The devotees’ preparations were dragging on, and he could not wait to see the Lord; so he hurried to Puri alone, taking with him only the Bengali brahmana Kamalakanta, a devotee of Sri Chaitanya (CC, Madhya 10.93–94). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that this was a brahmana of Navadvipa, a companion of the Lord — apparently the same whom the “Charitamrita” elsewhere calls Kamalananda (Adi 10.149). Thus these two reached Mahaprabhu ahead of all the other Bengalis.

“He came quickly and met the Lord, and the Lord rejoiced to have him there. Overwhelmed with love, the Lord bowed down at his feet; and Paramananda Puri, overwhelmed with love, embraced Him. The Lord said, ‘I long to live in your company. Be merciful to Me and make Niladri your home.’ Puri replied, ‘I too long to live in Your company. That is why I set out from Gauda and came to the city of Nilachala. When they heard that You had come back from the south, Shachi was overjoyed, and so were all the devotees. They are all coming to see You, but since they were delayed, I hurried on ahead.’” (CC, Madhya 10.95–100)8

The Lord lodged him in a secluded room in the house of Kashi Mishra and gave him a servant (CC, Madhya 10.101). Soon Svarupa Damodara came; having bowed to the Lord and to Nityananda, he respectfully bowed at the feet of Paramananda Puri too, and Puri embraced him with love (10.128). And Ramananda Raya, returning to the Lord in Puri, paid his respects to those gathered around Him — Nityananda, Paramananda Puri and others.

How the Lord Received Him in Puri

Vrindavana Dasa Thakura tells of Paramananda Puri’s coming in his own way:

“Some days later, having travelled to the holy places, Paramananda Puri came and met the Lord. Seeing Paramananda Puri from afar, Lord Gauranga respectfully rose. The Lord was overjoyed to see His dear devotee. He offered him due respect and began to dance in ecstatic love. Raising His arms, the Lord cried out: ‘Hari! Hari! At last I have seen Paramananda Puri with My own eyes. Today My eyes and My whole life have become perfect. Today I have gained the fruit of fulfilling all My religious duties.’ The Lord went on: ‘Today I have received the fruit of accepting sannyasa, for Madhavendra Puri has appeared before Me.’ Saying this, the Lord embraced His dear devotee, whose body was at once drenched with the tears flowing from Mahaprabhu’s lotus eyes. Paramananda Puri too was filled with bliss and forgot himself on seeing the moonlike face of the Lord. Thus they offered respects to each other. Paramananda Puri was the abode of pure love for Sri Chaitanya.” (CB, Antya 3.167–175)

The Lord, supremely pleased, accepted him among His intimate companions, and Puri, having found his Lord, joyfully served His feet (CB, Antya 3.176–177). One of the biographies says that from then on, whenever Mahaprabhu caught sight of Puripada even from afar, He would respectfully rise.9

Kavi Karnapura in his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” paints this meeting differently. The Lord, thinking of Paramananda Puri, calls him a disciple of Madhavendra “into whom, they say, has entered all the divine power” of His elder brother Vishvarupa.10 In Karnapura, Puri comes from Varanasi and longs so for the Lord that he hurries to Him before the darshan of Jagannatha, begging Jagannatha’s forgiveness: “You, the all-knowing, know Yourself what this thirst is.” The Lord rises, bows to him and asks: “Svamin, are you Puri-ishvara?” (act 8). In the same act Karnapura plays on his name: the call offstage about “the lord of Paramananda-puri” bearing his staff refers both to Jagannatha, Lord of “the City of Supreme Bliss,” and to the sannyasi with his danda. And when the Gaudiya devotees came to Puri, the Lord, presenting him to Advaita, said: “This Puri-ishvara is like a second Munindra, for he is the beloved disciple of your guru. Bow down to him” (Munindra, “the lord of sages,” is Madhavendra Puri), — and Advaita, and after him all the others, bowed to Puri; and, left alone with him and Svarupa, the Lord says that today He is fulfilled.

In Karnapura’s mahakavya, Paramananda Puri, wandering, comes to the Ganga, to Navadvipa, and stays in the Lord’s house. Shachi, “the mother of the three worlds,” honoured him with alms as her own son; the next day he accepted alms from Acharyaratna. Kamalananda, a beloved servant of the Lord, came there too, and after a few days they set out for Puri together with Gadadhara Pandita and Jagadananda; and the Lord Himself bowed to Puri, “showing him great respect as an elder” (13.110–125). Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” likewise says that he came before the Snana-yatra with Kamalananda (11.28–29) — and Kamalananda, according to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, is apparently the Kamalakanta of the “Charitamrita”; the “Karcha” of Govinda Dasa names him among the sannyasis who gathered around the Lord in Nilachala (3.501–504).11

Life with the Lord

From then on Paramananda Puri lived constantly with Mahaprabhu. He spent every chaturmasya with Him and took part in all His pastimes. He first stayed at Kashi Mishra’s house and afterwards settled in his own matha west of the Jagannatha temple, where he also dug a well; Vrindavana Dasa calls the place “the matha of Puri Gosani” (CB, Antya 3.232). He lived for the Lord alone, and the Lord held him dear as life itself; every day Puripada went first to see the Lord and only then turned to his other affairs.

Vrindavana Dasa writes that among the sannyasis around the Lord none was so dear to Him:

“Among the sannyasi companions of Sri Chaitanya there was none dearer to the Lord than Paramananda Puri. Paramananda Puri and Svarupa Damodara were the two most eminent devotees among all Mahaprabhu’s sannyasi companions. These two were always inseparable from Mahaprabhu. They took sannyasa to assist His pastimes as a sannyasi. Paramananda Puri was always absorbed in meditation, and Sri Svarupa always sang kirtana. These two sannyasis were like the arms of Lord Chaitanya.” (CB, Antya 10.46–49)

Puri’s “meditation” is not impersonal contemplation but absorption in the remembrance of Krishna. And Svarupa, says Vrindavana Dasa, the Lord loved just as He loved Paramananda Puri (10.42); elsewhere he calls the two of them “the chief companions of the Lord in His final pastimes” (Antya 3.181), and already at the beginning of his book, in the summary, he mentions how they settle in Puri to live with the Lord (Adi 1.161).

With Paramananda Puri the Lord had a special intimacy:

“The Lord and Paramananda Puri had a very confidential relationship, exactly like that of two close friends, Krishna and Arjuna. The Lord always delighted in Paramananda Puri’s company, holding confidential conversations with him about Krishna.” (CB, Antya 3.233–234)

Krishnadasa Kaviraja says the same, listing the branches of Sri Chaitanya’s tree in Puri:

“Of all the devotees who lived with the Lord in Nilachala, two were foremost, the Lord’s very heart: Paramananda Puri and Svarupa Damodara.” (CC, Adi 10.124–126)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta makes this a subheading of his “Anubhashya”: “The foremost — (1) Sri Paramananda and (2) Sri Svarupa.”12 Paramananda Puri is named among those who settled with the Lord in Puri (Madhya 1.252–254) and among the companions with whom the Lord went every morning for the darshan of Jagannatha (Madhya 15.184).

And in the conversation with Ramananda Raya, Krishnadasa Kaviraja reveals which rasas the Lord tasted with His closest ones:

“Puri's love was chiefly parental; Ramananda's was pure friendship; Govinda and others had the rasa of pure servitude; and Gadadhara, Jagadananda and Svarupa knew the bliss of the chief rasa.” (CC, Madhya 2.78)

According to one of the biographies, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains here that Paramananda Puri, the Uddhava of Krishna’s pastimes, loved Mahaprabhu with parental love. Both Puri’s vatsalya and his friendly intimacy with the Lord, like that of Krishna and Arjuna, are not worldly feelings of a “father” or a “companion,” but the pure rasas of an eternal associate, which the Lord Himself relishes.

Vrindavana Dasa repeatedly glorifies the Lord precisely as the treasure of Paramananda Puri: “Glory to Him who has become the wealth of the heart of Sri Paramananda Puri” (CB, Adi 14.2); “Glory to Gaurasundara, dearer than life itself to Paramananda Puri and Svarupa Damodara!” (Madhya 6.4); “You are the very life of Sri Paramananda Puri!” (Madhya 11.2); “All glory to Him who is the life and soul of Paramananda Puri!” (Antya 7.3). So too His devotees sing of the Lord: Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami in the “Shachisunu-ashtaka” praises the Lord “beloved of Paramananda Puri, accepting Govinda’s service, surrounded by Svarupa’s love” (2–3), and Narahari in a song sees the Lord in Nilachala holding sankirtana on the seashore “with Svarupa, Rupa, Ramananda, Govinda and Paramananda.”

The Well Filled with the Ganga

Vrindavana Dasa, “the Vyasa of the Lord’s pastimes,” glorifies Paramananda Puri’s well especially in the third chapter of the Antya-khanda of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata.” Beside his matha Puripada had dug a well, but its water turned out to be bad, and this grieved him. One day the Lord came to the matha of Puri Gosani and sat down beside him. The indwelling Lord of all, He knew Himself that the water was unfit, but, as if in passing, He asked Puri how the water in the well was. And Puri replied: “This well is most unfortunate: its water has become like thick mud” (CB, Antya 3.237).

“Hearing this, Chaitanya said: ‘Alas, Lord Jagannatha has become a miser. Even the most sinful of sinners is liberated if he touches the water of Paramananda Puri’s well. Therefore the maya of Lord Jagannatha has spoiled this water, so that no one may drink it.’” (CB, Antya 3.238–240)

This is a loving jest of the Lord, and it glorifies the well and Puri himself. So holy is this devotee’s water that whoever touches or drinks it will be purified and liberated — and so Jagannatha, as it were, “grew miserly”: He did not want liberation to be had so easily, and made the water muddy Himself. “Jagannatha’s maya” here is not worldly illusion with which the Lord might harm people, but His will and internal potency, yogamaya, which serves His pastimes.13

“Saying this, Mahaprabhu Himself rose, raised His arms and said: ‘O Lord Jagannatha, grant Me this boon: let the Ganga enter this well. Please command the Bhogavati Ganga, who flows through Patala, to enter this well.’” (CB, Antya 3.241–243)

So the Lord asked Jagannatha for mercy on the jivas. Hearing these words, the devotees loudly sang the names of Hari, and the Lord went home, and all lay down to sleep.14

“Then, obeying the Lord’s command, Gangadevi entered this well and filled it. The next morning all were astonished: Paramananda Puri’s well was filled with crystal-clear water.” (CB, Antya 3.246–247)

The Ganga, who springs from the Lord’s feet, at His command invisibly entered the well of His devotee. The devotees sang the name of Hari, and Puri Gosvami fainted with bliss. Understanding that the Ganga had come into the well, all began to bow to it and walk around it (CB, Antya 3.248–249).

Hearing of this, the Lord hurried to the well and, seeing the clear water, was filled with great joy:

“The Lord said: ‘Listen, devotees: whoever bathes in the water of this well will certainly obtain the benefit of bathing in the Ganga: he will attain pure loving service to Krishna.’” (CB, Antya 3.251–252)15

The Lord Himself, in great jubilation, drank this water and bathed in it (3.254), and, as one of the biographies says, did so often. And then He said of Puri Gosani:

“‘Know that I abide on earth only because of Puri Gosvami’s love. I belong to Puri Gosvami — have no doubt of it. If he wishes, he may even sell Me. Anyone who sees Puri Gosvami even once will become worthy of love for Krishna.’” (CB, Antya 3.255–257)

So speaks of Himself the Lord who is subject to the love of His devotees. He is the independent Master of all, and no one can “sell” Him; but by His own will He gives Himself to those who love Him — this is His bhakta-vatsalya, His tenderness towards His devotees, not dependence.

“Having told everyone of the glory of Paramananda Puri and sanctified his well, the Lord returned home. Only the Supreme Lord knows how to increase the glory of His devotees.” (CB, Antya 3.258–259)

Thus Lord Mahaprabhu sang the glory of His devotee. The Ganga in Puri’s well is not a miracle for its own sake, but the Lord’s mercy towards His servant and towards all jivas. The devotee sings the Lord’s glory, and the Lord in turn magnifies the glory of His devotee — a glory that those indifferent to the Lord cannot grasp. He makes His devotees great so that all may understand: without their company and their mercy the jiva cannot attain any good.

Paramananda Puri’s well is in Puri to this day. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, according to one of the biographies, writes in his commentary on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” that it lies not far from the Jagannatha temple, on the road leading west, near the police station, and that Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura identified it as the very well of which Vrindavana Dasa speaks.16

Intercessor for the Junior Haridasa

Paramananda Puri’s seniority among the Lord’s companions is vividly seen in the story of the Junior Haridasa, a singer with the Lord in Puri. Because he had spoken with a woman, Mahaprabhu cast him off and barred him from His house:

“‘From today you must keep this order of Mine: do not let Chota Haridasa come here.’” (CC, Antya 2.113)

For three days Haridasa ate nothing. Svarupa Damodara and other close devotees came to plead for him, but the Lord answered them sternly and told them never to speak of it again (CC, Antya 2.115–126). Then on the next day all the Vaishnavas went to Paramananda Puri: the Lord honoured him, His guru’s godbrother, as a guru, and they hoped that his word would help.17

“Then Puri Gosani came alone to the Lord. The Lord bowed to him and seated him with reverence. The Lord asked, ‘What is your order? Why have you come?’ Puri Gosani petitioned Him to show grace to Haridasa. Hearing this, the Lord said, ‘Listen, Gosani: stay here with all the Vaishnavas, and give Me leave to go to Alalanatha. I will stay there alone, with only Govinda.’ Saying this, the Lord called Govinda, bowed to Puri, rose and set off.” (CC, Antya 2.129–133)

The Lord did not grant the request, yet neither would He argue with an elder: honouring him, He chose rather to leave Himself.18 Puri was abashed; he hastily stood before the Lord and humbly begged Him to come back into the room:

“‘Do whatever You wish: You are the independent Lord. Who can tell You anything? All Your dealings are for the good of the people. None of us can know Your deep heart.’” (CC, Antya 2.135–136)

With these words Puri went home. The Lord did not forgive Haridasa: from then on he could only see Him from afar, when the Lord went to Jagannatha (2.137–142).

Puri’s humility in saying, “You are the independent Lord,” is not the failure of an intercessor but an example for all: the elder whom the Lord honours as a guru himself bows before the Lord’s will. And the Lord’s severity is not anger but a lesson to the world, as Krishnadasa Kaviraja says:

“Mahaprabhu is an ocean of mercy — who can understand Him? He punishes His own devotee to make people understand dharma.” (CC, Antya 2.143)

And by honouring Puri even while refusing him, the Lord taught something more: the guru’s godbrother deserves the same reverence as the guru, and disregard for the elders, the guru-varga, is ruinous for bhakti. Of this the Lord also speaks to Sanatana:

“‘Jagadananda is not dearer to Me than you. But I cannot bear a breach of propriety.’” (CC, Antya 4.166)19

At the Festivals of Nilachala

Paramananda Puri was beside the Lord in almost all His pastimes in Purushottama: at the cleansing of the Gundicha temple, at the Ratha-yatra, in the water-sports on Lake Narendra, at the festival after the passing of Haridasa Thakura. The Gaudiya Vaishnavas and the people of Puri all revered him as an elder worthy of worship.

When the Lord and His devotees washed the Gundicha temple before the Ratha-yatra, He did not ask the elders, the guru-varga, to carry water: they washed the temple with water that others carried.

“Except for Nityananda, Advaita, Svarupa, Bharati and Puri, everyone filled pots and brought water.” (CC, Madhya 12.109)

Damodara here is Svarupa Damodara, and Bharati is Brahmananda Bharati.

At the Ratha-yatra, when the chariot stopped, the Lord honoured the elders before all others, with His own hand marking their foreheads with sandal paste and adorning them with garlands:

“Paramananda Puri and Brahmananda Bharati received sandalwood paste from His holy hand, and their joy grew.” (CC, Madhya 13.30)

In the water-sports on the Narendra, says Vrindavana Dasa, “Nityananda, Gadadhara and Puri Gosvami began to fight one another in the water, but none of them was ever wholly defeated” (CB, Antya 8.122). Together with Nityananda and Gadadhara, Puri went with the Lord to meet Advaita and the Gaudiya devotees (CB, Antya 8.55). And at the festival in memory of Haridasa Thakura, “The Lord took His meal with Puri and Bharati, and then all the Vaishnavas ate.” (CC, Antya 11.87).

When the Gaudiya devotees had gone home after the Ratha-yatra, Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya asked the Lord and the ten sannyasis who were always with Him to take their meals at his house for a whole month: Paramananda Puri, Svarupa Damodara, Brahmananda Puri, Brahmananda Bharati, Vishnu Puri, Keshava Puri, Krishnananda Puri, Nrisimha Tirtha, Sukhananda Puri and Satyananda Bharati (CC, Madhya 15.193). Five days he set aside for the Lord Himself and five for Paramananda Puri; Svarupa, Sarvabhauma’s close friend, would come both with the Lord and on his own, and the other eight sannyasis twice each (15.194–196).20 For five days Paramananda Puri alone was feasted with mahaprasada in Sarvabhauma’s house.

The “Charitamrita” mentions him in many other scenes. He comes to the Lord soon after His return to Puri (Madhya 1.129); the sannyasis headed by him wait for the Lord to dine after His meeting with the Gaudiya devotees, and the Lord eats together with him, Brahmananda Bharati and Nityananda (Madhya 11.33, 11.197–211); he is with the Lord at the meal in the garden by the Gundicha (12.156); at the Netrotsava he and Brahmananda Bharati walk before the Lord (12.208);21 he comes to Advaita’s feast (14.92); he is named first among the companions with whom the Lord sets out from Puri to Gauda on the way to Vrindavana (16.127); on the Lord’s return from Vrindavana he and Brahmananda Bharati are the first to bow to Him at the Narendra-sarovara (25.220). The Lord introduces Sanatana Gosvami to him (Antya 4.104–108); the sannyasis headed by him partake of Vallabha Bhatta’s maha-prasada (Antya 7.62); the Lord sends prasada to him and to Brahmananda Bharati (Antya 16.105); and the cloth-prasada from Jagannatha’s festival of the cowherd pastimes the Lord, “on the advice of Paramananda Puri,” would send to His mother (Antya 19.12).22

Murari Gupta names him among the companions who went out with the Lord to the Narendra-sarovara to meet the Gaudiya devotees (4.17.17), among those who were with the Lord when a poor brahmana from Dravida came to Him, “in the circle of Svarupa and his companions, Sri Paramananda Puri, Ramananda and others” (4.21.12), and among His companions in Puri (4.24.13); in the water-sports on the Narendra Gaura appears as the One “who has Paramananda Puri, Vamshi and Ramananda as His helpers” (4.18.15), and in the table of contents of his poem Murari recalls both the meeting in the South and how the Lord “sent Sri Paramananda Puri away to the Kshetra” (4.25.25–26). Lochana Dasa adds that it was Puri Gosani who asked the Lord about this poor brahmana (CM, Shesha-khanda, pt. 7, vv. 85–86).

In Karnapura’s “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” the Lord, returning from Vrindavana, meets Paramananda Puri and Svarupa and addresses him: “Teacher!” — the company of such as he, says the Lord, is sweeter even than the service of other tirthas; and Puri answers that only by good fortune were they not burned up in the forest fire of separation from the Lord (act 9). In the same act Sarvabhauma tells the king that only five or six went with the Lord towards Gauda, and names Puri-ishvara first. In the tenth act the Lord sits with Puri-ishvara, talks with him and Svarupa about the king and about Advaita, goes with him to meet the Gaudiya devotees, and of Shivananda Sena’s little son says to him: “Svami, this is your servant” — a hint at the boy’s name, Puri-dasa, “servant of Puri”: so the author of the drama himself was called as a child. When the Lord goes to Jagannatha, on either side of Him are Puri-ishvara and Svarupa; at the Ratha-yatra Puri-ishvara is “the beholder before the Lord Himself”; and at the Hera-panchami festival, when Svarupa says that Lakshmi’s procession shows the rasa of fury (raudra), Puri answers him: “for the onlookers this is the rasa of wonder.” In Karnapura’s mahakavya Paramananda Puri at the Ratha-yatra drinks in the beauty of the dancing Lord, bathed in tears (16.30).

Ramachandra Puri

Once Ramachandra Puri, another disciple of Madhavendra, came to Puri. The Lord and Paramananda Puri honoured him as a disciple of their guru:

“Paramananda Puri paid homage at his feet, and Puri Gosani embraced him firmly. Mahaprabhu offered him prostrate obeisance; he embraced the Lord and remembered Krishna. For some time the three of them spoke together about the Lord. Then Jagadananda Pandita invited him for a meal.” (CC, Antya 8.6–8)

Ramachandra Puri, however, looked for faults in everything and reproached the Lord for eating much. The Lord began to eat half as much as before. Then Paramananda Puri, together with all the devotees, humbly entreated Him:

“‘Ramachandra Puri has the nature of a fault-finder. What will be gained by giving up food at his word?’” (CC, Antya 8.70)23

Ramachandra Puri, he said, himself makes people overeat and then reproaches them; of the two rules of the “Bhagavatam” — not to praise and not to blame others (11.28.1) — he keeps only the first: he praises no one but blames everyone; in one who has a hundred virtues he sees none. “Accept all our invitations as before,” Puri begged (Antya 8.71–81). The Lord defended Ramachandra Puri, but, yielding to their entreaties, began to eat half of what He had eaten before (8.82–84). Thus Paramananda Puri, while honouring his godbrother, saw his fault clearly and cared only that the service of the Lord should not suffer.

Chataka-parvata

Once, seeing the sand-hill Chataka-parvata in Puri, the Lord took it for Govardhana and ran towards it in ecstasy. The devotees rushed after Him:

“Puri Gosani and Bharati Gosani came to the seashore, and the lame Bhagavan Acharya followed very slowly.” (CC, Antya 14.90)

Puri and Bharati arrived later, when the Lord was already coming to Himself:

“Meanwhile the two, Puri and Bharati, arrived. Seeing them both, Mahaprabhu was filled with reverence. When He came fully into external consciousness, the Lord offered His respects to them both, and the two embraced Mahaprabhu with love. The Lord said, ‘Why have you two come so far?’ Puri Gosani said, ‘To see Your dancing.’ At Puri's words the Lord was embarrassed.” (CC, Antya 14.113–116)

On the Way to Gauda, and in Other Traditions

When the Lord set out from Puri for Gauda, Paramananda Puri went with Him. Karnapura in his mahakavya tells of this journey in detail: with the Lord go Govinda, Jagadananda, Damodara Pandita and Paramananda Puri (19.6); the sanctified cloth received from Prataparudra the Lord sent to His mother, accepting Puri’s advice (19.9); at dawn “Puri-prabhu” covered with a cloth the mark of a blow from a book on Damodara Pandita’s back (19.30); when the Lord nearly fell on thorns, Puri and others caught Him (19.47); the Lord stays with him in a freshly plastered house (19.55); the Lord and Puri walk in front, Ramananda behind (19.60); a local brahmana invites Puri to a meal (19.70). And when people asked, “Where is Krishna-Chaitanya?”, the Lord and Puri in jest pointed at each other (20.7). From Raghava’s abode the Lord sent “the elder” ahead to Navadvipa — apparently Paramananda Puri (20.13).

Lochana Dasa relates that when, on this journey, the Lord unexpectedly turned back from Natashala Kanai, Paramananda Puri asked Him the reason, and the Lord explained: the wish of Nrisimhananda’s mind had been fulfilled — he had paved a road for Him in his mind from Purushottama to Mathura, but had brought it only as far as Natashala Kanai (CM, Shesha-khanda, pt. 2, section “The Lord Sees Vrindavana,” v. 22). According to Lochana too, Puri Gosani, with the devotees in Kashi Mishra’s house, begged the Lord to receive King Prataparudra, who had fasted for ten days, and the Lord agreed (pt. 6, vv. 92–110).24 Lochana Dasa also praises him at the beginning of the poem — “Puri Paramananda and Vishnupuri … I praise” (Sutra-khanda, pt. 1, v. 26) — and calls him “Paramananda Puri of pure conduct” (Sutra-khanda, pt. 8, v. 624).

Jayananda, in the opening vandana of his “Chaitanya-mangala,” bears on his head “Srinivasa, Paramananda Puri, Vishnu Puri, Madhavendra Puri, Ishvara Puri,” and, describing the memorial festival for Madhavendra Puri at Advaita’s house in Shantipura, says: “Damodara Svarupa and Paramananda Puri direct the feast, canes in hand.” The late “Prema-vilasa,” to be approached with caution, reports that Madhava Acharya (Kavivallabha), who had fled from his wedding to Vrindavana, took sannyasa from Paramananda Puri and afterwards learned bhajana from Rupa and Sanatana (24.436; 25.891).25

In Narahari Chakravarti's “Namamrita-samudra,” where the Lord's associates are invoked one after another, there is a verse for him too — together with Brahmananda:

“O Brahmananda, Sri Paramananda Puri! Hold me by the hair and keep me always on the path of bhakti.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 45)

After the Lord’s Disappearance

Paramananda Puri outlived Mahaprabhu. When, after the Lord’s disappearance, Srinivasa Acharya came to Puri, he stayed with Gadadhara Pandita and met there Ramananda Raya, Sarvabhauma, Vakreshvara, Paramananda Puri, Shikhi Mahiti, Govinda, Shankara, Gopinatha Acharya and others; all of them, plunged in separation from the Lord, had almost given up food and sleep, and all of them blessed him (“Bhakti-ratnakara” 3). When and where Paramananda Puri himself passed away is not known.

According to the “Sri Gaudiya-vaishnava-abhidhana,” Paramananda Puri wrote a book, the “Govinda-vijaya.” Jayananda speaks of it still earlier: “Sri Paramananda Puri Gosani, the venerable, set [this] out briefly in the ‘Govinda-vijaya.’” The book itself has not survived — at least, it is unknown to us.

Significance

Paramananda Puri is the Uddhava of Krishna’s pastimes, the central root of the tree of bhakti, and one of the “two arms” of the Lord as a sannyasi. The Lord Himself says that He abides on earth only because of his love, and promises love for Krishna to anyone who sees him even once. Together with Svarupa Damodara he was the very life of Sri Chaitanya in Nilachala, and with him the Lord tasted the sweetness of parental love.

Through him the Lord showed the world how to honour one’s elders. His connection with Madhavendra Puri made Paramananda Puri an object of the highest reverence for the Lord: the Lord bowed to him, rose to meet him, was the first to adorn him with sandal paste and garlands, and even when refusing his request did not forget to honour him. The guru’s godbrother deserves the same reverence as the guru, and disregard for the guru-varga is ruinous for bhakti.

And through him the Lord showed how He glorifies His devotees. The Ganga in Puri’s well, the words “I belong to him,” and the promise of love for Krishna to those who see him — all this the Lord says and does so that the world may understand: without the company of devotees and their mercy the jiva has no good. And the supreme secret of the tree of bhakti of which the “Charitamrita” speaks is that the Lord Himself is both the gardener and the trunk on which all the branches rest; and among the roots on which the tree is established, the central one is Paramananda Puri.
